objectives: Trace how a torn vessel seals itself: vascular spasm, the platelet plug, then the fibrin net.
Explain how the clotting factors switch each other on, from two ways in through factor X and thrombin to fibrin, and how antithrombin and plasmin hold the clot in check.
Name exactly where heparins, warfarin, factor Xa inhibitors and direct thrombin inhibitors act on the cascade.
Tell antiplatelet drugs and thrombolytics apart from anticoagulants by what they act on.

heparin.prompt: Heparin latches on to antithrombin, the natural brake, and makes it switch off thrombin and factor Xa much faster. What happens to the fibrin net?
choices: It thins: less thrombin is left to make fibrin
It thickens: the brake pushes more fibrin out
It stays the same: heparin acts only on platelets
It dissolves at once, like a clot-busting drug
heparin.why: Heparin does not touch fibrin directly. By speeding the antithrombin brake it leaves less factor Xa and thrombin working, so less fibrinogen becomes fibrin and the net thins.

vka.prompt: Warfarin blocks the liver's recycling of vitamin K, which the liver needs to finish factors II, VII, IX and X. What goes out into the blood?
choices: Clotting factors that are made but cannot work
No clotting factors at all
Extra clotting factors, to make up for the loss
Normal factors that are broken down faster
vka.why: The liver still makes the proteins, but without vitamin K it cannot add their finishing touch, so they cannot work. The brakes proteins C and S are made faulty the same way.

xa.prompt: A factor Xa inhibitor sits on switched-on factor X and stops it working. Which steps below it are affected?
choices: Thrombin and fibrin: less of both is made
Only the platelet plug, which shrinks
None: thrombin is made straight from tissue factor
Only plasmin, which speeds up
xa.why: Factor Xa is the first step of the shared path, the step that makes thrombin. Block it and less thrombin is made, so less fibrin too.

dti.prompt: A direct thrombin inhibitor blocks thrombin itself, while factor X still switches on as usual. What happens to fibrin?
choices: Little is made, because thrombin cannot turn fibrinogen into fibrin
It is made as usual, because factor X is working
It is made faster, because thrombin is freed up
dti.why: Fibrinogen becomes fibrin only through thrombin. With thrombin blocked, factor X working upstream does not help: the net barely forms.

antiplatelet.prompt: Aspirin stops platelets making thromboxane, and P2Y12 blockers stop ADP landing on platelets. Both are signals stuck platelets use to call in more. What happens to the platelet plug?
choices: It is smaller and looser: fewer platelets are called in
It is bigger: the signals pile up
It is the same: these drugs act only on clotting factors
antiplatelet.why: With one signal silenced and the other unable to land, fewer passing platelets join. The plug is smaller and looser, and it offers less surface for the cascade.

lytic.prompt: A thrombolytic turns plasminogen into plasmin. What does plasmin do to an unwanted clot?
choices: Cuts up its fibrin net, so the clot breaks up
Adds fibrin to make it stronger
Stops new platelets joining, but leaves the clot alone
Switches off factor X, so no new thrombin forms
lytic.why: Plasmin is the enzyme that breaks down fibrin. Making more of it breaks up a clot that has already formed, which no anticoagulant or antiplatelet drug can do.

quiz.stem: What forms the first, soft seal over a small tear in a vessel?
choices: A plug of platelets stuck together
A net of fibrin threads
A clump of red blood cells
A layer of antithrombin
quiz.why: Platelets pile into the tear first. Fibrin comes later and knits that soft plug into a firm patch.

quiz.stem: What helps platelets stick to the collagen exposed by a tear?
choices: Von Willebrand factor, which acts like double-sided tape
Antithrombin, which glues them on
Plasmin, which roughens the collagen
Thrombin, which turns platelets into fibrin
quiz.why: Von Willebrand factor binds both collagen and the platelet, holding the platelet on. Antithrombin and plasmin work against clotting, not for it.

quiz.stem: Where do the two ways into the cascade meet?
choices: At factor X, the first step of the common pathway
At fibrinogen
At plasmin
At the platelet plug
quiz.why: Tissue factor with factor VII, and contact through factors XI and IX, both switch on factor X. From there one shared path makes thrombin and then fibrin.

choices: Switches off thrombin and factor Xa, keeping the clot at the wound
Turns prothrombin into thrombin
Cuts fibrin threads apart
Makes platelets stickier
quiz.why: Antithrombin is the cascade's main brake: it switches off thrombin and factor Xa. Cutting fibrin is plasmin's job, a separate clean-up.

choices: They speed up antithrombin, which switches off thrombin and factor Xa
They block the recycling of vitamin K in the liver
They stop platelets making thromboxane
They turn plasminogen into plasmin
quiz.why: Heparins work through antithrombin. Blocking vitamin K recycling is warfarin, stopping thromboxane is aspirin, and making plasmin is a thrombolytic.

quiz.stem: A patient takes warfarin. Which proteins does the liver release in a form that cannot work?
choices: Factors II, VII, IX and X, and proteins C and S
Only fibrinogen
Only antithrombin
Factors VIII and XIII
quiz.why: These are the vitamin K–dependent proteins: four clotting factors and two of the cascade's brakes. Fibrinogen, antithrombin and factors VIII and XIII do not need vitamin K.

quiz.stem: A patient takes aspirin after a heart attack. What does it act on?
choices: Platelets: it stops them making thromboxane
Factor Xa, which it blocks directly
Thrombin, which it blocks directly
Fibrin, which it dissolves
quiz.why: Aspirin is an antiplatelet drug: without thromboxane, platelets call in fewer others. It does not act on the clotting factors or on fibrin.

quiz.stem: A clot is already blocking an artery. Which kind of drug breaks it down?
choices: A thrombolytic, which makes plasmin to cut the fibrin
A factor Xa inhibitor, which dissolves fibrin
An antiplatelet drug, which dissolves platelets
Vitamin K, which reverses clotting
quiz.why: Anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs stop new clot forming; only a thrombolytic, by making plasmin, breaks down fibrin that is already there. Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not a clot.

takeaways: A torn vessel seals itself in three moves: the wall squeezes, platelets plug the tear, and fibrin knits the plug into a firm net.
Platelets stick to exposed collagen with von Willebrand factor's help, then call in more with ADP and thromboxane.
The cascade is a chain of switches: tissue factor with VII, and contact through XI and IX, switch on factor X; Xa turns prothrombin (II) into thrombin, and thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin.
Antithrombin switches off thrombin and factor Xa; plasmin cuts fibrin away as the vessel heals.
Heparins work through antithrombin. Warfarin blocks vitamin K recycling, so factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S are made faulty.
Factor Xa inhibitors block factor Xa directly; direct thrombin inhibitors block thrombin itself.
Antiplatelet drugs act on platelets: aspirin stops thromboxane, P2Y12 blockers block ADP's landing site. Thrombolytics make plasmin to break up a clot that has already formed.
